blocks.text: On entering he almost fell, for behind the door there was one more step. “They don’t show the public much consideration,” he said. “They show no consideration at all,” said the usher, “just look at the waiting room here.” It was a long corridor, from which roughly carpentered doors led to the separate compartments of the attic. Although there was no direct access of light, it was nevertheless not completely dark, for some of the compartments had, on the side facing the corridor, instead of solid plank walls, mere wooden lattices, reaching, it is true, up to the ceiling, through which some light penetrated and through which one could also see individual officials, as they wrote at tables or stood right up against the lattice and watched the people in the corridor through the gaps. There were, probably because it was Sunday, only a few people in the corridor. They made a very modest impression. At almost regular intervals from one another they sat on the two rows of long wooden benches that were fixed along both sides of the corridor. All of them were negligently dressed, although most of them, to judge by their facial expression, their bearing, the cut of their beards and many small details that could scarcely be pinned down, belonged to the higher classes. Since there were no coat hooks, they had placed their hats under the bench, probably each following the example of the other. When those who sat nearest the door caught sight of K. and the usher, they rose in greeting, since those next to them saw this, they believed they too had to greet, so that all of them rose as the two went by. They never stood completely upright, their backs were bent, their knees buckled, they stood like street beggars. K. waited for the usher, who was walking a little behind him, and said: “How humiliated they must be.” “Yes,” said the usher, “they are accused men, all of those you see here are accused.” “Really!” said K. “Then they are my colleagues.” And he turned to the nearest one, a tall, slender man whose hair was already almost grey. “What are you waiting for here?” K. asked politely. The unexpected address, however, threw the man into confusion, which looked all the more embarrassing since he was evidently a man of the world who elsewhere certainly knew how to control himself and did not easily give up the superiority he had acquired over many. Here, however, he did not know how to answer so simple a question and looked across at the others as if they were obliged to help him, and as if no one could demand an answer of him should this help not be forthcoming. Then the usher stepped up and said, in order to calm and encourage the man: “The gentleman here is only asking what you are waiting for. Do answer.” The voice of the usher, probably familiar to him, had a better effect: “I am waiting —” he began, and faltered. He had evidently chosen this beginning in order to answer quite precisely to the question as it was put, but now could not find the continuation. Some of those waiting had drawn near and stood around the group, the usher said to them: “Away, away, clear the corridor.” They drew back a little, but not as far as their former seats. Meanwhile the man who had been questioned had collected himself and even answered with a slight smile: “A month ago I submitted some applications for evidence in my case, and I am waiting for them to be dealt with.” “You seem to be going to a great deal of trouble,” said K. “Yes,” said the man, “it is my case, after all.” “Not everyone thinks as you do,” said K., “I, for instance, am accused too, but, as I hope to be saved, I have neither submitted an application for evidence nor undertaken anything else of the kind. Do you really consider that necessary?” “I don’t know exactly,” said the man, again in complete uncertainty; he evidently believed K. was making a joke at his expense, and so, for fear of making some new mistake, he would probably have liked best to repeat his earlier answer in full, but under K.’s impatient gaze he said only, “as far as I am concerned, I have submitted applications for evidence.” “You don’t believe, I suppose, that I am accused,” asked K. “Oh please, certainly,” said the man, and stepped a little to one side, but in the answer there was not belief, only fear. “So you don’t believe me?” asked K., and, unconsciously invited to do so by the man’s humble manner, took him by the arm, as if he wanted to force him to believe. He did not want to cause him pain, and had only touched him very lightly, yet nevertheless the man cried out, as if K. had seized him not with two fingers but with red-hot tongs. This ridiculous screaming made K. finally weary of him; if they did not believe he was accused, so much the better; perhaps the man even took him for a judge. And now, by way of farewell, he really did grip him harder, pushed him back onto the bench and walked on. “Most of the accused are so sensitive,” said the usher. Behind them almost all of those waiting were now gathering around the man, who had already stopped screaming, and seemed to be questioning him closely about the incident. Coming towards K. now was a guard, recognizable chiefly by a sabre whose scabbard, at least to judge by its colour, was made of aluminium. K. was astonished at this and even reached out his hand towards it. The guard, who had come because of the screaming, asked what had happened. The usher tried to reassure him with a few words, but the guard declared that he must nevertheless see for himself, saluted, and walked on with very hurried but very short steps, probably measured out by gout.
